content: 1. Bacterial pericarditis is a condition where bacterial infection leads to inflammation of the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart. 2. Empiric antimicrobial therapy is initiated when bacterial pericarditis is suspected, even before specific pathogens are identified. 3. Purulent pericarditis, characterized by pus accumulation in the pericardial sac, requires immediate and aggressive treatment. Preferred regimen for purulent pericarditis: 4. Administer vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours, aiming for trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL, for a total duration of 28 days. Combine this with ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 28 days. Alternative regimens for purulent pericarditis: 5. Option 1: Vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL) for 28 days, combined with cefepime 2 g intravenously every 12 hours for 28 days. 6. Option 2: Vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL) for 14–42 days, combined with ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days. Specific considerations for purulent pericarditis: 7. For purulent pericarditis associated with contiguous pneumonia, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL), combined with either ceftriaxone 1–2 g intravenously every 12 hours or cefotaxime 2 g intravenously every 6–8 hours, and either ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours or levofloxacin 500–750 mg intravenously every 24 hours. 8. For purulent pericarditis associated with contiguous head and neck infections, the preferred regimen is either imipenem 500 mg intravenously every 6–8 hours or ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g intravenously every 6 hours. 9. For purulent pericarditis secondary to infective endocarditis, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL) combined with gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day intravenously every 8–12 hours. Pediatric considerations for purulent pericarditis: 10. After cardiac surgery, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 6 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL), combined with either ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day intravenously every 12–24 hours or cefotaxime 200–300 mg/kg/day intravenously every 6–8 hours, and gentamicin 6–7.5 mg/kg/day intravenously every 8 hours. 11. For purulent pericarditis associated with genitourinary infections, the same pediatric regimen as above is recommended. 12. For immunocompromised pediatric patients, the same regimen as above is also recommended. Culture-directed antimicrobial therapy for bacterial pericarditis: 13. For penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, the preferred options include penicillin G 5–24 million units per day intramuscularly or intravenously every 4–6 hours for 14–42 days, cefotaxime 2 g intravenously every 6–8 hours for 14–42 days, ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days, or levofloxacin 500–750 mg intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days. 14. For penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, the preferred options include ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days, levofloxacin 500–750 mg intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days, or vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL) for 14–42 days. 15. For methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), the preferred options include nafcillin 1–2 g intravenously every 4 hours for 14–42 days, oxacillin 1–2 g intravenously every 4 hours for 14–42 days, cefazolin 1–2 g intravenously every 48 hours for 14–42 days, vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL) for 14–42 days, or clindamycin 600–900 mg intravenously every 8 hours for 14–42 days. 16. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), the preferred options include vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours (targeting trough levels of 15–20 μg/mL) for 14–42 days or linezolid 600 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days. 17. For Neisseria meningitidis, the preferred options include penicillin G 5–24 million units per day intramuscularly or intravenously every 4–6 hours for 14–42 days, cefotaxime 2 g intravenously every 6–8 hours for 14–42 days, or ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days. 18. For Gram-negative bacilli, the preferred options include ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days, levofloxacin 500–750 mg intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days, or cefepime 2 g intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days. 19. For anaerobic bacteria, the preferred options include clindamycin 600–900 mg intravenously every 8 hours for 14–42 days, metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg intravenously every 6 hours for 14–42 days, or ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g intravenously every 6 hours for 14–42 days. 20. For Mycoplasma pneumoniae, the preferred options include doxycycline 100 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days or azithromycin 500 mg intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days. 21. For Legionella pneumophila, the preferred options include ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–42 days, levofloxacin 500–750 mg intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days, or azithromycin 500 mg intravenously every 24 hours for 14–42 days. Viral pericarditis treatment: 22. For cytomegalovirus (CMV) pericarditis, administer immunoglobulin at a dose of 4 mL/kg on days 0, 4, and 8, followed by 2 mL/kg on days 12 and 16. 23. For Coxsackie B virus pericarditis, use interferon alpha or beta at a dose of 2.5 million IU/m² of body surface area subcutaneously three times per week. 24. For adenovirus and parvovirus B19 perimyocarditis, administer immunoglobulin 10 g intravenously on days 1 and 3 over a 6–8 hour infusion period. Fungal pericarditis: 25. Fungal pericarditis requires antifungal therapy tailored to the specific fungal pathogen identified.
